newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank profits seen buoyant, except Deutsche.
newsitem.headline: German bank profits seen buoyant, except Deutsche.

text.p: Most of Germany's top banks are expected to report buoyant 1996 profit growth with one big exception -- giant Deutsche Bank AG, which suffered a series of blows including trouble at its London-based Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM).
"Overall, banks profited from buoyant market conditions last year," said Olaf Conrad, banking analyst at Morgan Stanley in London.
"But I'm cautious for 1997 because I can't imagine the favourable conditions will last all year."
Deutsche reports key 1996 data on Tuesday at 0700 GMT and analysts put its net profit at 2.17 billion marks ($1.3 billion) on average, up three percent from the 1995 result of 2.1 billion marks.
Munich-based Bayerische Vereinsbank AG, Germany's fourth-largest bank, also announces results on Tuesday and is expected to report net profit of 759 million marks on average, up 15.5 percent.
Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG follows on Wednesday and analysts expect a net profit of 660 million marks, down 2.3 percent due to an expected strong rise in risk provisions.
Results for Dresdner Bank AG, Germany's number two bank, are due on Thursday. Analysts expect a 30 percent jump in net profit to 1.57 billion marks.
Commerzbank AG, the third largest bank, last month reported a 22 percent rise in net profit.
Conrad predicted earnings at Germany's top five banks would grow 10 percent on average in 1997, with Deutsche likely to outperform Dresdner and Commerzbank.
He said that forecast will have to be raised if markets continue the rally they have staged so far this year.
Deutsche was hit by the estimated 200 million-pound cost of compensating investors for alleged mismanagement at three MGAM unit trusts by former MGAM fund manager Peter Young.
The bank plans to take the payment onto its 1996 books but analysts see little direct impact on earnings because Deutsche is expected to have dissolved some reserves to foot the bill.
But the problem at MGAM, which came to light last September, was only the latest in a string of problems for Deutsche last year.
The bank is estimated to have added more than 200 million marks to risk provisions to cover a bail-out of engineering group Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG (KHD).

Also, two major shareholdings, Daimler-Benz AG and construction group Philipp Holzmann AG, omitted dividends for 1995, costing Deutsche 219 million marks in lost income, according to analysts' estimates.
Earnings have also been squeezed by sharp gains in administration costs as Deutsche throws money at its investment banking business and restructures its domestic branch network, analysts said.
While booming financial markets are helping to boost banks' trading income, analysts warn that earnings from their traditional business of lending money and taking deposits remain under pressure.

In a sign of concern over the prospect for tighter competition and narrower lending margins, Moody's Investors Service last week put Dresdner on review for a possible downgrade of its triple A long-term debt rating.
Dresdner is the last remaining German private sector bank with a top rating from Moody's.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.692 German Marks)
